Like many other birders across Nova Scotia, I’ve been enjoying going out to find all the migrants that are now in the province for the warmer months. I always think of these birds’ long journeys and how they’ve flown thousands of kilometres to spend the summer with us all. How lucky we are.

But those birds are at greater risk than ever before thanks to climate change.

“Nearly two-thirds of North American bird species are vulnerable to significant range loss if the planet warms 3°C (5.4°F) above pre-industrial temperatures,” according to this briefing from Climate Central, a group of scientists and communicators who research and report on climate change.

There’s more. From the Climate Central briefing:

Shorter winters, spring warming, and earlier first spring leaves can disrupt the annual cues that birds rely on to begin their migrations.

These disruptions may impact the long-term survival of bird populations — making the future uncertain for hundreds of species across North America.

Indeed, the total North American bird population has lost a staggering 2.9 billion birds since 1970 — a 29% decline. The vast majority of individuals lost were birds that migrate. And common backyard birds like sparrows, warblers, blackbirds, and finches saw the most severe decline.

Here’s a list of 35 birds in Nova Scotia that are highly vulnerable to a 3°C of warming of the planet.

There are other species found in N.S. that will lose a considerable amount of range at a 3°C of warming. They include:

John Kearney is a retired social anthropologist who lives in Yarmouth County. He’s also been a birder since the age of 13. He writes about issues of conservation, climate change, birds, and bird migration on his website, here.

On June 7, Kearney published this post titled, “Climate Change and Severe Weather: How Can We Mitigate the Effects on Birds?”

Kearney and I spoke in May about his work and what he’s learning about severe storms and their effects on migratory birds.

“By the early 2000s, I was feeling pretty convinced that climate [change] was changing things,” Kearney said.

In October 2005, when Kearney was working at St. FX, he was out birdwatching and chimney swifts started flying overhead.

“They’re out of here by August,” Kearney said. “September at the latest.”

This wasn’t long after Hurricane Wilma went over the province. Kearney said about 700 chimney swifts were found dead. You can read about that here.

It wasn’t the first time Kearney heard about a similar die-off. Kearney said when he was an undergrad student at Acadia University, there was a large die-off of chimney swifts on the campus.

“At that time, we didn’t think of it in terms of climate change,” Kearney said. “Just a weird thing.”

But the die-off of the chimney swifts in 2005 was the first time such a die-off was documented. You can read about that here.

Between the fall of 2005 and the spring of 2006, the population of chimney swifts was down by 50%. Still, Kearney said there was some controversy over the numbers since there was also a decline in aerial insects around the same time. Chimney swifts feed on aerial insects.

“That was sort of not really ever resolved,” Kearney said. “I thought it was the hurricane that did this. But that doesn’t necessarily mean climate change. It could just be the hurricane.”

Of course, since then the severity and frequency of hurricanes has increased.

“That’s where I began to think we need to look at this more closely,” Kearney said.

Kearney talked about two disasters in Nova Scotia that affected birds. In October 2017, Kearney said he detected several species of warblers, including magnolia warblers and American redstarts, flying overhead at night.

“They were supposed to be gone,” Kearney said.

The next morning, Kearney said he awoke to learn there was a fallout of hundreds of birds, including scarlet tanagers, red-eyed vireos, and cat birds, which were supposed to be further south, but were still in Nova Scotia. Kearney said this fallout was also noticed in New England.

Kearney said he and other members of the Nova Scotia Bird Society wrote a paper on the weather at the time.

“We determined that over Tampa, Florida there were severe thunder storms with severe updrafts,” Kearney said.

“The birds were on their way and about to cross over Cuba to South America, they got caught in these updrafts, they couldn’t get down, and they got swept out over sea and hit these very strong northeasterly winds that drove them straight up to Nova Scotia. This was an almost unheard of situation.”

The following year in March, Kearney said 58 great blue herons, green herons, and egrets were found on Sable Island. Zoe Lucas with the Sable Island Institute wrote about that event here.

“Some of them were alive but within a few hours they just dropped dead,” Kearney said.

Kearney said there was an extra tropical cyclone that formed an eye like a hurricane. The herons got caught in the eye of that storm and flew in the eye up to Nova Scotia.

“They were able to jump off at Sable Island,” Kearney said. “So, here again, this was a big event, but still people were saying this was a one-off. A couple of us did think this was maybe a sign of climate change.”

Kearney said there are two empirical studies that show this is an actual issue. Those studies, which you can read here and here, show how severe climate change-related storms affect birds.

Kearney told me about a multi-year study of juvenile tiger sharks in the Gulf of Mexico that found 39% of those tiger sharks had songbirds such as warblers, thrashers, sparrows, and orioles in their bellies.

That study also looked at weather patterns at the time. You can read about that study here.

“These were birds having to deal with strong winds, getting tired, and falling into the ocean,” Kearney said. “They were an easy meal for juvenile tiger sharks. I said this is another clue.”

Kearney said an event known as “The Great Texas Freeze” killed half of the population of purple martins after a snow storm hit the state after the birds returned to their nesting sites.

“These are just some examples,” Kearney said. “There are so many factors that affect birds that you can’t be absolutely sure. Reason will tell you that it’s got to be climate change.”

There were more events like the wildfires in California in 2020 where birds that were so stressed by the heat they flew to other states like Nevada to try to build up their reserves. But the food they needed wasn’t as abundant.

That same fall, Kearney said there was a cold snap.

“All those birds either died right then or those who still had some energy flew to New Mexico where they found one million emaciated birds,” Kearney said.

Kearney wrote about these storms and the birds they affected in his blog post from June 7.

He also included a list of actions to mitigate the effects of severe storms on birds and their habitats. Here’s the list, although Kearney has more details in his post:

Kearney writes in his post:

I view this list as an initial attempt to develop a comprehensive management plan to protect birds and their coastal habitats in Nova Scotia from severe weather. Much more is needed to build on this outline and implement an effective plan. The Nova Scotia government’s failure to proclaim the Coastal Protection Act and its backsliding in creating high-quality protected areas are the exact opposite of the recommendations in the scientific literature. I hope this essay will guide us in reversing course and advancing our conservation efforts to create an environment more resilient to climate change, especially as it pertains to birds.

Kearney said many birders do go out in hurricanes — I don’t — since those storms bring birds to the province they may not see otherwise. He said those storms are a chance for birders to keep the data on what birds they see.

“To help us understand better what the birds are going through and how we might help them,” Kearney said.

Long-term care workers at St. Vincent’s Nursing Home in Halifax have voted on a tentative deal. That’s according to this press release from the Canadian Union of Public Employees (CUPE) on Thursday. From the press release:

CUPE long term care workers have been on strike since April 13th. They weresuccessful in fighting for a minimum $5 raise for all workers over the life of the collectiveagreement, additional wages for supervising and training students, and improved layoffprotections.

All other striking CUPE locals will hold their own ratification votes in the coming daysand weeks, and if members accept the deal, it will officially bring the province-widestrike to an end.

In last week’s Morning File, I wrote about taking part in Hiking Buddies, a program led by Milena Khazanavicius, who is blind and advocates for accessibility, and Janet Barlow of Hike Nova Scotia.

This past Saturday, I joined Khazanavicius as her sighted guide during White Cane and Guide Dog Awareness Walk in downtown Halifax. The walk was hosted by Khazanavicius and Laura Bain, a program coordinator at CNIB.

I quickly learned the barriers for blind and partially sighted people are far different in the city than during a walk in a park. First of all, one of the main barriers are other people! I personally felt like I was back working on the dancefloor section of The Dome, however, I wasn’t holding a tray of drinks above my head, getting burned with cigarettes, or getting my butt grabbed by someone.

What I didn’t notice were the issues Sue Uteck, executive director of the Spring Garden and Area Business Association, said are creating havoc on the street. Philip Moscovitch wrote about that here in Thursday’s Morning File.

The sidewalks are a dirty mess, though, as Tim Bousquet has written about before.

Khazanavicius had her guide dog, Hope, along for the walk. Hope is always a hit with people. Fortunately, people didn’t stop to pet or distract Hope since she’s a working dog, after all.

Before I met up with Khazanavicius, Bain, and the rest of the group, I noticed there were five Halifax Regional Police (HRP) cruisers blocking off Sackville Street at the corner of and South Park Street.

Anyway, our group headed out from the main gates at the Public Gardens and headed down Spring Garden Road to Queen Street. We crossed the street to the Central Library and then walked back up Spring Garden on the other side. There were more cops at all the intersections, and Spring Garden was closed to traffic.

I was describing our surroundings, including all the cops, to Khazanavicius. We decided a dignitary was in town.

I didn’t take many photos as I was busy paying attention. But I did get this photo of the parade that I later learned was part of the Festival of Chariots, which also had music, food, and other events at the Garrison Grounds. This explained all the cops who had the streets blocked off for the event.

Our group also got our own tour of the Public Gardens. Our guide James was fantastic and crafted a tour of the gardens that allowed everyone to touch, feel, and smell the plants, trees, and flowers.

We got to feel the scars on the trees that were axed by a still unknown vandal in July 2023. We touched some of the silky flowers on the rhododendrons, and felt the leaves on the ginkgo biloba. James did a great job describing all the details of the plants, trees, and statues.

Khazanavicius told me that Vision Mates is always looking for volunteers. That’s a program offered by CNIB that matches people who are blind or partially sighted with sighted guides. A few of the sighted guides who joined the group on Saturday were new. Here’s a bit about Vision Mates from the program website:

Vision Mate volunteers can assist individuals with various activities, including errands, going for walks, labelling and organizing household items, reading, or fun outings and recreational activities.

Matches are made with someone who lives close to your home, school or work! Most visits happen once a week, for one to two hours, at a time and place that works for both of you.

When making a match, we take into account location, availability, age, gender, and shared interests. We hope each match lasts at least six months, and many go much longer.

Honestly, this is a great idea and I encourage others to sign up. Khazanavicius said sighted guides are needed in other areas in HRM, including Lower Sackville.

Khazanavicius told me the next training session for Vision Mates is June 29 from 6pm to 8:30pm at the CNIB office on Almon Street.

Madiha Mughees reports:

This month, the Nova Scotia government will begin pesticide spraying to curb the spruce budworm outbreak in spruce and fir forests of northwestern Cape Breton (Pleasant Bay), including a portion of the Polletts Cove – Aspy Fault Wilderness Area.

Spruce budworm is considered a highly destructive pest with population outbreaks every 30 to 40 years.

Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki (Btk) is the pesticide selected by the government to manage the outbreak.

“Btk is a naturally occurring biological microbe that has been used worldwide for decades,” Robert Strang, chief medical officer of health of the province, said in a recent statement. “It has been studied extensively and been approved by Health Canada for organic farming.”

As Mughees writes, in May the province announced the treatment would take place primarily on Crown lands, however, they forgot to mention that a portion of Polletts Cove – Aspy Fault Wilderness Area will also be sprayed. That’s a protected area.

From Mughees’ story:

But during an information session on Tuesday evening, Sean Power, manager of private land programs, scaling, and forest health with the Department of Natural Resources (DNR), mentioned that 838 hectares (3%) of the 27,230 hectares in the Polletts Cove – Aspy Fault Wilderness Area will also be sprayed.

“As climate change continues to stress our forests and amplify the risks of wildfire and long-term ecological damage, the urgency of maintaining this strategy cannot be overstated,” Power said.

While the Nova Scotia government is proceeding with the plan, Parks Canada, which manages the Cape Breton Highlands National Park under federal jurisdiction, has opted out.

On a related note, this Facebook video by Shane Abernethy with the Tommy Thompson Park Bird Research Station, which is part the Toronto and Region Conservation Authority, talks about the Cape May warbler. That’s a warbler than breeds in Canada’s boreal forests and eats spruce bud worm. So, the warbler’s populations rise and fall with spruce bud worm outbreaks.

However, that’s only a temporary benefit, or a “phantom population gain,” as Abernethy says, since the spruce bud worm will kill the boreal forests that the birds rely on.

I recommend you watch Abernethy’s videos of the birds he bands and tracks. I want his job.

Click or tap here to read “Nova Scotia to spray pesticide to kill Spruce budworm in Cape Breton, including inside a wilderness area.”

This morning, we published part 2 of Euan Thomson’s 11-month investigation into the. dismantling of Halifax-based Out of the Cold Community Association. You can read part one here.

Part two looks at the role Halifax Regional Police (HRP) played in the closure of the shelters. From the story:

Two reasons may explain why Halifax police appeared eager to get Out of the Cold out of the picture.

First, as recently as February 2026, Halifax police were eyeing up the land that houses the modular shelter and Centennial Pool as one of three possible locations for their new headquarters — and the only option on the Halifax peninsula. The city councillors representing the local wards have been clear about their support for preserving the pool, which has received a groundswell since the initial 2022 council motion to close it. The current police headquarters is across the street, and recent reporting in the Halifax Examiner appears to confirm the Centennial-shelter site remains a contender, with a $180 million budget.

Second, in the government’s August 14, 2023 email to Out of the Cold leadership threatening to withdraw funding, an executive director in the provincial Department of Community Services, Joy Knight, referred to evidence that Out of the Cold staff had “obstructed police responses to emergency calls” at the Halifax shelter and demanded a more “collaborative” relationship with Halifax police.

In its August 25 reply, Out of the Cold denied this as a “serious allegation that goes against our police policy,” asked the government to provide evidence, explained that Halifax police have a “fraught relationship with homeless people,” and expressed concern that its residents could be “further criminalized, injured, or killed by violent police action.”

Thomson also interviewed Carlo Cininni, who was a frontline worker with Out of the Cold, about his experiences with HRP during his time working with the organization.

Click or tap here to read “Out in the Cold, Part 2: Shelter staff ‘treated like criminals’ by politically motivated police.”

On Friday night, I attended a Tiny Church Concert at the Little Dutch Church on Brunswick Street. I’ve been to the church before and am fascinated by its history. You can read about the church here.

A few weeks ago, I learned about the Tiny Church Concerts, which features various musicians and singers from around the region. They put on a one-hour show at the church, and the cost is by donation. Friday night’s show featured The Rabbit Town String Band, who are fantastic. Offering this venue as a stage for local talent is such a great idea. Plus, the show was over well before my bedtime.

I will definitely attend again. You can check the schedule of concerts here.

re: coal mine and birds.
The Donkin coal mine on Cape Breton Island was developed on Cape Perce, a globally significant bird and biodiversity area. The forest was prematurely clear-cut to allow for future coal waste piles and the ongoing noise and light pollution is a hazard for migratory and breeding birds.

Local birds seem to be doing reasonably well.  We even have had an extended family of Ravens move into our yard.  Our resident Crow familiy is not thrilled and are trying to force the Ravens down the road a bit.

We are seeing some migratory birds coming, but not in the numbers of pevious years – we have our Osprey, Bald Eagle and Great Blue Herron families all returing and doing well.

Thanks for the article on the hazards of being a migratory bird. Many people have noticed the steep reduction in the numbers of birds around. Not necessarily fewer species (though probably that too) but definitely fewer individuals of most all species.
